newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Space commander's heart skips a beat under strain.
newsitem.headline: Space commander's heart skips a beat under strain.

text.p: Vasily Tsibliyev, the commander of Russia's Mir space station, has spent his life flirting coolly with danger as a Soviet airforce pilot and cosmonaut.
But this week, the 43-year-old's heart finally skipped a beat as he struggled with preparations for a risky repair job in space after the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history.
"There was an indication of arrhythmia," Mission Control's chief doctor Igor Goncharov announced on Tuesday, explaining there was a tiny irregularity in Tsibliyev's heartbeat.

Yet it was a bombshell that set ground staff scrambling to reschedule the repairs. Finally, on Wednesday, they pulled Tsibliyev from the job, leaving NASA physicist Michael Foale to step in to help engineer Alexander Lazutkin next week.
"It came as a surprise," Tsibliyev coolly told Mission Control of the slight palpitation he had felt at the weekend.

To the common man back on Earth, it seemed anything but surprising that five months in space, during which he has coped with a serious fire and a host of mishaps before the collision on June 25, had finally overstrained the vital organs of even the super-fit, super-trained space commander.
"Naturally the internal anxiety, emotional stress and the sense of responsibility which he is suffering are all having an effect on him," Goncharov said.
Mission Control officials neither confirm nor deny reports that Tsibliyev was responsible for last month's accident.
Arrhythmia can either be a relatively harmless and passing manifestation of stress or a life-threatening indication of a condition that can cause blackouts and even sudden death.
A Mission Control spokesman told Reuters on Wednesday that all the data pointed to the less serious form but that it was not possible to tell for sure while Tsibliyev was in orbit.
"Generally, there are two kinds of arrhythmia," said a doctor at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, where President Boris Yeltsin was treated after heart surgery last year.

"If it involves a change in the heart muscle it is serious, lasts for the rest of your life and the only treatment involves constant medication," said the doctor, who spoke on condition of anonymity. "In the second, linked to tension and tiredness, there is no change in the heart muscle, simply irregular beats.
"For this, you need a couple of weeks rest."

The Mission Control spokesman said: "Whether the heart muscle is affected, we cannot tell on the ground. From all the data we have, however, the irregularities are not connected with the muscle because he feels well, just nervously exhausted."
Tsibliyev is on a course of sedatives and Etmosin, a drug that is designed to counter irregular beating of the heart.

But the continuing strain of the mission seems to leave little room for a full recovery before two of the three crew must spend six hours or more in awkward and bulky spacesuits mending cables in the punctured and airless Spektr module.

If Foale, 40, who has none of Tsibliyev's long experience of spacewalks, is able to do the job, it should go ahead late next week with the commander taking the American's post in Mir's Soyuz escape capsule, ready to abandon ship if things go wrong.
It will be a testing few hours for a man trying to combat heart problems. If Tsibliyev did have difficulty with his heart muscle this would definitely be his last spell in space.
But Mission Control officials recalled others have come back from temporary injury -- like veteran cosmonaut Alexander Viktorenko, who was once electrocuted and passed out on Mir.

Tsibliyev's wife Larisa said last month her husband could trust to his training to pull him through. And if that did not work, he could count on the plastic bunny lucky charm his daughter gave him: "It's not pretty. But it always works."
